title: Complement closure of deterministic finite-testable counter languages
formal: For every one-way deterministic finite-testable multicounter machine M with a right endmarker, is there another such machine N over the same input alphabet Sigma with \(L(N)=\Sigma^*\setminus L(M)\)?
definitions: A machine has finite control and finitely many nonnegative integer counters, initially zero. A step consumes the next input letter, consumes the right endmarker, or is an epsilon step consuming nothing. It inspects one selected counter with guard zero, positive, or no guard, then changes that counter by −1, 0 or +1 and changes state. A decrement requires the positive guard. Input is read once from left to right; after the endmarker only epsilon steps are possible. A finite run accepts after consuming the entire input and endmarker if its state is final and all counters are zero. It need not be a maximal run. Determinism requires at most one enabled transition in every instantaneous configuration, including conflicts between epsilon and input-consuming steps. A machine is finite-testable if there exists a finite bound r such that each counter is explicitly tested zero at most r times on every accepting run. The bound is fixed for the machine, independent of input, and does not restrict nonaccepting runs. Positive tests and unguarded steps do not count toward r; final zero-counter acceptance is not an additional transition test. A word with no accepting finite run is rejected, even if its computation continues forever. N may use a different finite number of counters and test bound. This is language-class closure, with no required effective transformation or machine-size bound.
answer_criterion: Prove closure in Lean for all machines in the specified class, or construct one such language and prove that no deterministic finite-testable machine recognizes its complement. Complement recognition by a nondeterministic partially blind machine is insufficient for the positive direction.
context: The source separates deterministic closure from complement recognition with nondeterminism. Its latter construction does not settle the former.
why: This asks whether a limited zero-test resource preserves a basic language-theoretic closure property.
